The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Reflection can reveal what was suppressed, but identity also needs experiments. Try painting, dancing, gardening, a language, a sport, volunteering, music, or something else that has no obvious value to your résumé or social position. Notice what holds your attention when nobody is impressed.
brief:
- reflection can reveal what was suppressed, but identity also needs experiments in real life (keep "also": reflection still counts)
- try a specific new activity: painting, dancing, gardening, a language, a sport, volunteering, music, or something else (open examples)
- something with no obvious value to your résumé or social position ("obvious" hedges; social position means status, not social life)
- notice what holds your attention when nobody is impressed (attention is the signal, not talent or applause; enjoying praise isn't banned)
- context, not for the text: From Survival to Experimental Play already says people grow by trying things on and finding what you like when nobody's grading you, so don't explain that again
- context, not for the text: two drafts read AI in Pangram (0.90 for this one: "Reflection can show you what was suppressed, but for identity you also need some experiments out in real life. So try something new with no obvious value for your résumé or your status, like painting or dancing. Maybe you end up in the back of a dance class, watching somebody else's feet and counting under your breath. Notice what holds your attention anyway, when nobody is impressed."). Both carried the guide's three sentences in the guide's order (reflection isn't enough, try X, notice what holds your attention), so the paragraph reads as a sequence of steps even with a picture in the middle. Change the voice, not the words: say it the way the narrator would say it out loud to a friend. Stop inside the thought once, to react, to wonder what it would feel like, or to give the reader's own objection its own plain sentence.
